title: A desert watered by fog
hook: How does life find water among these dunes?
shortFact: In Namibia’s Namib Sand Sea, fog is the main water source for a specialised desert ecosystem. The dunes themselves contain material transported from inland by rivers, ocean currents and wind.
explanation: A desert can be extremely dry and still receive vital water without much rain. In the Namib Sand Sea, Atlantic coastal fog supplies moisture that specially adapted animals and plants can use. UNESCO describes a landscape whose small habitats shift with wind, sand and changing fog conditions. There is another hidden journey here: much of the sand did not simply weather out of the rock directly underneath it. Material travelled from the continental interior through a sequence of river transport, ocean movement and wind. Both the water supply and the dunes connect this apparently isolated desert to processes beyond it.

title: Everest and Chimborazo win different height contests
hook: Where you start measuring changes the winner.
shortFact: Everest is highest above mean sea level, but Ecuador’s Chimborazo has the summit farthest from Earth’s centre. Earth’s equatorial bulge gives Chimborazo an advantage despite its lower sea-level elevation.
explanation: Earth is not a perfect sphere: its rotation makes it wider around the equator. Chimborazo sits close to that bulge, while Everest is much farther north. If you measure altitude from mean sea level, Everest wins at about 8.85 kilometres, compared with Chimborazo’s roughly 6.27 kilometres. If you instead measure from the centre of Earth, Chimborazo’s summit is about 2.1 kilometres farther out than Everest’s. These are two different starting points, not contradictory answers. A diagram exaggerating the bulge can make the idea clearer, but the real planet’s departure from a sphere is much subtler than such an illustration suggests.
